sections.heading: Cache Organization & Mapping

entries.cue: Why do architectures use a memory hierarchy?
entries.notes: To balance trade-offs between access speed, storage capacity, and cost. High-speed SRAM caches sit close to CPU registers while slower, high-capacity DRAM acts as main storage.

entries.cue: What is the penalty of a cache miss vs cache hit?
entries.notes: Cache hits resolve in sub-nanosecond to a few nanoseconds (4-5 CPU cycles for L1). Cache misses require fetching from DRAM across the memory bus, taking 50–100 nanoseconds (~200+ cycles).

- Direct Mapped: Each block maps to exactly 1 cache line; simple and fast hardware, but prone to frequent conflict misses.
- Fully Associative: Blocks can reside in any line; eliminates conflict misses but requires complex, expensive parallel search hardware.
- Set Associative: Balanced hybrid where cache is split into sets with N ways (e.g., 8-way set associative).

entries.cue: Summary of cache levels, sizes, and latencies
entries.notes:
| Cache Level | Typical Size | Typical Latency | Location |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| L1 Cache | 32 KB - 64 KB per core | 1 - 2 ns (4-5 cycles) | On-chip (Core) |
| L2 Cache | 512 KB - 1 MB per core | 3 - 5 ns (12-14 cycles) | On-chip (Core) |
| L3 Cache | 16 MB - 64 MB shared | 10 - 20 ns (40-60 cycles) | On-chip (Shared) |
| Main DRAM | 16 GB - 128 GB | 60 - 100 ns | Off-chip DIMMs |

sections.summary: CPU caches bridge the multi-order-of-magnitude speed disparity between fast processor cores and high-capacity DRAM using multi-tier L1/L2/L3 caches with set-associative placement.

sections.heading: Locality Principles & Optimization

entries.cue: What are Temporal vs Spatial Locality?
entries.notes:
1. Temporal Locality: Memory accessed once is likely to be accessed again soon (e.g. loop index variables, repeated functions).
2. Spatial Locality: Memory items physically adjacent to recently accessed items are likely to be accessed soon (e.g. contiguous arrays).
